assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength optical lattice proposal made it possible to interrogate many neutral atoms Doppler- and recoil-free at optical frequencies, and the resulting clocks now reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is a clean, original instrument-level invention in laser spectroscopy and precision measurement, the kind of 'what we can measure, and how accurately' advance that I regard as central to atomic physics, with reach into geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a prospective redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori originated the lattice-clock concept and its magic-wavelength condition; Jun Ye's group demonstrated and pushed the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability and connected it to frequency combs. A two-person prize is natural. Credit from the broader community (Hall and Hansch were already recognised for combs; ion-clock work by Wineland's group, single-ion Al+ clocks, and other lattice-clock groups) is outside the supplied names and must be handled by framing the citation narrowly.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs worldwide operate lattice clocks and agree at the 1e-18 level; the interpretation is stable and the impact is already demonstrated. Recognition would be timely, with no premature-confirmation concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to frame the prize around optical clocks more broadly, which could bring in ion-clock pioneers not on this credited list.
I am recalling clock-performance numbers from memory and have not verified them here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum logic with trapped ions turned a speculative idea into a concrete, experimentally accessible architecture, and Blatt's group and others realised gates, entanglement and algorithms with high fidelity. Conceptually original, technically demanding, and foundational for quantum computing and simulation. Wineland and Haroche's 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, so a new prize must be justified by the computation-specific contribution.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive 1995 theoretical proposal; Blatt is the leading experimental realiser in Innsbruck, with Wineland's NIST group and others also central (Wineland already a laureate). A theory-plus-experiment trio is a plausible configuration, though credit for early experimental gates is shared more broadly than the three names.
assessment.maturity: Trapped-ion quantum computing has been replicated by many groups and is commercial-scale; the core concepts are very mature. Recognition is timely, with some concern about overlap with the 2012 prize.
uncertainties: How far the 2012 prize already covers this ground.
Whether experimental credit beyond Blatt (e.g., other ion-trap leaders) is adequately captured by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms provides inertial, gravitational and fundamental-constant measurements of exceptional sensitivity, from gravimeters and gradiometers to tests of the equivalence principle and measurements of the fine-structure constant. It is a strong, concrete case of measurement science built on laser cooling and coherent atom optics.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's Ramsey-Bordé interferometer theory and early work, Pritchard's early atom interferometers and Kasevich's atom-interferometric inertial sensors are all substantial. Credit is complicated by names absent from this list (Chu and others; Chu already shared the 1997 prize partly for laser cooling) and by priority questions among early demonstrations, so a fair configuration needs care.
assessment.maturity: Highly confirmed by many groups, with field-deployable devices, though the largest fundamental-physics payoffs are still developing. Recognition is mature enough but could be argued either way.
uncertainties: Disputed priority among early interferometer demonstrations.
Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 prizes for cooling and Bose-Einstein condensation, which enabled this field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light allow measurement below the standard quantum limit, and their routine use in gravitational-wave detectors is a tangible, widely recognised application of quantum optics to precision measurement. Caves's theory of quantum-limited interferometry and the later experimental squeezing and detector implementation form a coherent narrative.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the 1981 theory; Kimble's group and the Bell Labs group (Slusher and colleagues, not in the supplied names) produced early experimental squeezing; Schnabel contributed to GEO600/LIGO-compatible squeezed-light implementations. The supplied names omit key experimentalists, so the allocation is unclear.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is now operational in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 and is well confirmed, though the cleanest prize story ties it to the 2017 gravitational-wave prize and may be seen as downstream of it.
uncertainties: Missing experimental pioneers outside the credited list.
Whether the committee would view this as an enabling technology rather than a stand-alone discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter quantum interfaces, including atomic-ensemble quantum memories, entanglement of distant ensembles and cavity QED-based nodes, underpin quantum networks and repeaters. The physics is deep and original, drawing on coherent light-matter interaction, slow light and electromagnetically induced transparency. I work in a neighbouring area (rare-earth-doped crystal memories), so I weigh this carefully and do not claim special neutrality; the topic is also broader than any single decisive discovery.
assessment.attribution: Polzik (continuous-variable ensemble entanglement and memories), Kimble (cavity QED and quantum-network proposals) and Lukin (EIT-based storage and quantum-repeater/network architectures) each contributed distinct elements, with major contributions from others as well (for example Hau's slow light, Lukin and Fleischhauer's EIT proposals, and solid-state memory groups). A fair three-person configuration is not obvious, and this is a compound topic.
assessment.maturity: Individual demonstrations are well confirmed, but a practical quantum memory or repeater with high efficiency and long storage is still developing, so the field is arguably still in progress and the prize case somewhat early.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit across many groups and platforms, including solid-state memories.
Whether performance and applications are mature enough.
My own research proximity to this field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition and quantum-gas microscopy with single-site resolution. This created a new quantum-simulation platform for strongly correlated matter, built on the atomic physics toolkit of laser cooling and trapping.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and others) gave the key theoretical proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices; Greiner and Bloch performed the 2002 Mott-insulator experiment and developed quantum-gas microscopes. Credit also belongs to others (Jaksch, Bakr, Greiner's colleagues and the Hänsch group's early lattice work) not in the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated and active, yet the strongest scientific payoff is still developing as simulators tackle open problems; a good case but arguably still maturing.
uncertainties: Overlap with other candidates crediting the same people (Bloch, Zoller).
Whether quantum simulators have yet solved a landmark open problem.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Coherent optical readout and control of single nitrogen-vacancy centre spins in diamond opened solid-state quantum sensing at the nanoscale, with room-temperature operation, from magnetometry and thermometry to biological probes and quantum-network nodes. It connects directly to sensing individual quantum objects.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko achieved single-NV optical detection and coherent control; Lukin's group extended this to quantum registers, sensing proposals and applications. Others (for example Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Budker and the Walsworth group) contributed major steps, which complicates the three-name set.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed with commercial devices, but many applications are still emerging, and the discovery has a diffuse set of key contributors.
uncertainties: Broad community credit beyond the three names.
Whether the strongest results are single-spin physics or applications still in development.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics created strong coupling between superconducting qubits and microwave resonators, enabling dispersive readout and the architecture used in most superconducting quantum processors. It is original, clear and extremely influential.
assessment.attribution: Blais and Schoelkopf with colleagues (Girvin, Huang, Majer and others) proposed and developed the architecture, and Wallraff demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. Girvin and Devoret are conspicuously absent from the supplied names, and Devoret was a 2025 co-laureate for related superconducting-circuit work, so it is unclear how a fair triple would be drawn.
assessment.maturity: Heavily confirmed and widely adopted, but the recent prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, as I recall it, may reduce near-term appetite.
uncertainties: Missing key contributors such as Girvin.
Overlap with the most recent prize for superconducting circuits, which I recall but have not verified here.
